title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
This incident is an instance of a model asserting fabricated information as fact, specifically a legal AI tool generating case citations, quotations, and legal holdings that do not exist. The failure occurred at the drafting stage of litigation, when an attorney used an AI tool called Irys under the mistaken belief that it was connected to her firm's established legal research subscription. Seven nonexistent case citations appeared across eight filed court documents before opposing counsel, not the filing attorneys, detected the problem.

The failure would have been caught by a routine verification step: checking each cited case against an authoritative legal database before filing. No such check was performed. The attorney's mistaken assumption about the tool's connection to a trusted research service meant the output was treated as verified when it was not. This is a deployment outside the conditions the tool was intended or understood to be used for, compounded by the absence of a human review step before submission to a court.

What is not established is whether the AI tool itself was defective, whether the law firm or the tool's developer bore any specific legal responsibility, and what sanctions if any the court imposed. The lawyers admitted to the fabrications, but an admission of error is not a finding of professional misconduct or a judicial ruling on consequences.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
# Summary

Lawyers representing State Farm in a Los Angeles lawsuit have admitted to using artificial intelligence that generated fake legal cases and citations in their court filings. The homeowner, Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, sued State Farm after a 2020 fire made her Carson home uninhabitable, followed by water damage during repairs. After State Farm delayed approving repairs, construction never completed, forcing her family to drain savings, declare bankruptcy, and lose their home to foreclosure. The homeowner's attorney discovered that State Farm's lawyers included cases that do not exist, nonexistent quotes, and false legal holdings in their motions.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted she used an AI tool called Irys, mistakenly believing it was connected to her law firm's legal research subscription, and confirmed seven case citations across eight filings simply did not exist. This incident reflects a broader problem in the legal industry, where 41 percent of law firms now use generative AI. A global database has documented 1,922 legal hallucinations, with most occurring in the United States. The case proceeds to trial in October 2024.
